content: The diagnostic assays currently available for tuberculosis (TB) have suboptimal sensitivity, making them unsuitable as general diagnostic tools for TB. However, these assays demonstrate improved sensitivity for diagnosing TB in individuals co-infected with HIV, particularly in those with low CD4 cell counts. Among these, the lateral flow urine lipoarabinomannan (LF-LAM) assay, specifically the Alere Determine TB LAM Ag (referred to as Alere LAM), is the only commercially available urinary LAM test. This test has potential utility as a rule-in diagnostic tool for TB in patients with advanced HIV-induced immunosuppression, facilitating the early initiation of anti-TB treatment. The World Health Organization (WHO) strongly recommends the use of LF-LAM to assist in diagnosing active TB in HIV-positive adults, adolescents, and children who either present with signs and symptoms of TB (pulmonary and/or extrapulmonary) or have advanced HIV disease or are seriously ill. Advanced HIV disease in adults, adolescents, and children aged 5 years or older is defined as a CD4 cell count of less than 200 cells/mm³ or the presence of a WHO clinical stage 3 or 4 event. All children under 5 years of age with HIV are considered to have advanced disease. Seriously ill is defined by the presence of at least one of four danger signs: respiratory rate >30/min, temperature >39°C, heart rate >120/min, or inability to walk unaided. The WHO also suggests using LF-LAM in HIV-positive individuals with TB symptoms or those who are seriously ill, but this recommendation is conditional due to low certainty in the evidence regarding test accuracy. Conversely, WHO recommends against using LF-LAM in HIV-positive individuals without TB symptoms or without assessing TB symptoms, particularly in those with unknown CD4 counts or CD4 counts ≥200 cells/mm³, due to very low certainty in the evidence. The Alere LAM test is a point-of-care immunocapture assay that detects lipoarabinomannan (LAM), a lipopolysaccharide component of the mycobacterial cell wall, in urine. LAM is released from metabolically active or degenerating mycobacterial cells during TB disease. The test is performed manually by applying 60 µL of urine to the test strip, incubating it at room temperature for 25 minutes, and visually inspecting the strip for bands. The intensity of visible bands is graded using a manufacturer-supplied reference scale. The test is simple to use, requires minimal training, and is stable for up to 15 months at 30°C. The diagnostic accuracy of Alere LAM varies by setting and patient population. For HIV-positive adults with TB symptoms: In inpatient settings, sensitivity is 52% (40–64%) and specificity is 87% (78–93%). In outpatient settings, sensitivity is 29% (17–47%) and specificity is 96% (91–99%). Across all settings, sensitivity is 42% (31–55%) and specificity is 91% (85–95%). For HIV-positive adults irrespective of TB symptoms: In inpatient settings, sensitivity is 62% (41–83%) and specificity is 84% (48–96%). In outpatient settings, sensitivity is 31% (18–47%) and specificity is 95% (87–99%). Across all settings, sensitivity is 35% (22–50%) and specificity is 95% (89–98%). For adults with advanced HIV disease (CD4 ≤200 cells/mm³), irrespective of TB symptoms: In inpatient settings, sensitivity is 64% (35–87%) and specificity is 82% (67–93%). In outpatient settings, sensitivity is 21% (8–48%) and specificity is 96% (89–99%). Across all settings, sensitivity is 26% (9–56%) and specificity is 96% (87–98%). For adults with CD4 ≤100 cells/mm³: In inpatient settings, sensitivity is 57% (33–79%) and specificity is 90% (69–97%). In outpatient settings, sensitivity is 40% (20–64%) and specificity is 87% (68–94%). Across all settings, sensitivity is 47% (30–64%) and specificity is 90% (77–96%). For HIV-positive children, limited data suggest: Sensitivity ranges from 42% to 56%, and specificity ranges from 80% to 95%, depending on the study and setting. The WHO emphasizes that LF-LAM should be used as an adjunct to clinical judgment and in combination with other diagnostic tests. It is not intended to replace existing diagnostic methods or serve as a triage test. The reviewed evidence and recommendations apply specifically to the Alere LAM assay, as other LAM-based assays have not been adequately validated for widespread use.
